data.title: 16-Year-Old Suspected KillSec Ransomware Leader Arrested As Police Seize 110TB Of Stolen Data
data.description:
KillSec Infrastructure Seized As Teen Suspected Of Leading Ransomware Group Is Arrested

A 16-year-old suspected of being the main operator of the KillSec ransomware group has been arrested in Spain as international authorities moved to take down the infrastructure behind around 1,000 suspected cyberattacks.

The operation also saw authorities seize five servers, take control of KillSec's leak site and secure at least 110 terabytes of stolen data, preventing the information from being accessed or published by the group.

‼️ BREAKING: A 16-year-old is suspected of running the KillSec ransomware group, Europol says.

Police seized KillSec's leak site, securing at least 110TB of data. Three suspects were provisionally arrested and eight properties searched in Greece, Romania, Spain and the UK.

The… pic.twitter.com/GE72emJ6YA

— International Cyber Digest (@IntCyberDigest) October 1, 2026

Teen Suspected Of Running KillSec Arrested In Spain

The teenager, described by Europol as the suspected administrator and main operator of KillSec, was arrested in Alicante, Spain, on 30 September 2026.

Reuters reported that he is a Romanian national.

Two other suspects were also arrested, bringing the total number of provisional arrests to three, while police searched eight properties across Spain, Greece, Romania and the UK.

The investigation was led by German authorities through the Hamburg State Criminal Police Office and Hamburg Public Prosecutor's Office, with support from authorities across Europe and the US.

The operation involved Belgium, Finland, Germany, Greece, the Netherlands, Romania, Spain, Switzerland, the UK and the US, alongside Europol and Eurojust.

Cybersecurity firms Bitdefender and Group-IB also provided technical support during the investigation.

16 year old Romanian Masterminded KillSec - then is Arrested

Spanish police and Europol arrested a 16-year-old Romanian national in Alicante as the suspected main operator of the KillSec ransomware group, part of Operation KillSwitch that seized the group’s leak site, five… pic.twitter.com/TLOgGEk0xk

— DeepTape (@DeepTapeNews) October 2, 2026

110TB Of Stolen Data Secured As Leak Site Falls

Authorities took control of KillSec's dark-web leak site and secured at least 110TB of data linked to victims.

The site had been used to name organisations that KillSec claimed to have attacked and threaten them with the release of stolen files if they did not pay a ransom.

Europol said authorities also took control of domains operated by the group and redirected visitors to a law-enforcement seizure notice.

Five central servers used to manage the operation and store stolen victim data were also brought under police control.

Investigators are now examining the seized devices, infrastructure and data as they work to identify additional victims, attacks and people involved in the operation.

How Did KillSec Carry Out Its Attacks?

KillSec emerged in 2024 and gained access to organisations by exploiting software vulnerabilities and poorly secured entry points, particularly in cloud environments.

After infiltrating systems, the group copied sensitive information and moved it to infrastructure under its control.

⚠️#Ransomware⚠️Allegedly, #KillSecurity has named a new victim.#DarkWeb#Cybersecurity#Security#Cyberattack#Cybercrime#Malware#Privacy#Infosec

Country: #Bangladesh🇧🇩
Threat Actor: Kill Security aka KillSec
Company: Agrani Bank
Industry: Banking
Revenue: $92.8M
Data… pic.twitter.com/orgazTP6d4

— Dark Web Informer (@DarkWebInformer) May 16, 2024

#BREAKING Digital #threat actor 'Killsec' ransomware group alleged to impact #Chinese insurer Ping An; claims [all] exfiltrated data to be published October 15, 2024. #Asia 🖥️

SOURCE: https://t.co/5iQs6G8Jw6pic.twitter.com/lMfrIx3ZK5

— OSINTEL101 (@osintel101) October 9, 2024

Victims were then listed on KillSec's leak site and threatened with the public release of their files unless they paid.

According to Europol, investigators are looking into around 1,000 suspected attacks linked to KillSec worldwide, with about 500 so far identified as successful.

Around 70 of the suspected attacks involved government organisations.

The number could change as investigators continue analysing evidence seized during the operation.

#OperationKillSwitch, led by German authorities, with support from @Europol and Eurojust, has taken action against #KillSec, a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group linked to around 1,000 suspected attacks worldwide. The action targeted both the people behind KillSec and the… pic.twitter.com/C0KvmipOa4

— Group-IB Global (@GroupIB) October 1, 2026

KillSec Used Ransomware Tools To Target Organisations

The group's model allowed other cybercriminals to use its ransomware services and tools, according to researchers tracking the operation.

Halcyon previously described KillSec as offering a relatively low-cost ransomware-as-a-service platform, with a Tor-based control panel, chat functions and custom ransomware tools that could allow attackers with limited technical skills to launch operations.

🚨 KillSec launches new ransomware-as-a-service affiliate program

A ransomware group using the name "KillSec" is advertising what it describes as a new "borderless RaaS" platform designed to provide affiliates with ransomware infrastructure, management tools, and victim-handling… pic.twitter.com/srPK8xn4Hm

— Dark Web Informer (@DarkWebInformer) September 20, 2026

Bitdefender has tracked KillSec since 2024 and identified nearly 300 victims on its leak site.

The cybersecurity company said KillSec posted 126 victims in 2025 and 25 in 2026, with the latest victim appearing on 18 September, shortly before the law-enforcement operation.

Bitdefender researcher Alexandru Nicola Stoica said the group was "mostly opportunistic with its targets" and that the company did not have an estimate of victims' losses.

Investigators Also Found AI In KillSec's Operations

The investigation uncovered evidence that KillSec used artificial intelligence to help build and maintain its infrastructure and identify potential victims.

The finding adds another layer to an operation that already relied on cloud vulnerabilities, stolen data and dark-web infrastructure to carry out extortion.

Authorities had been investigating KillSec-linked attacks since early 2025, eventually identifying suspects believed to have taken on different roles within the group, including an administrator, developer, negotiator and affiliate.

One suspected developer turned 18 in August 2026 but was a minor when some of the alleged offences took place.

UK Arrest Linked To US Criminal Charges

The operation also led to the arrest in the UK of Dutch national Fouad Eltibrizi, who allegedly used the online name "Archduke".

The US Department of Justice indicted Eltibrizi on 16 September 2026 over an alleged role connected to the KillSec operation and charged him with conspiracy to commit unauthorised computer access.

UK authorities arrested him on 30 September and are preparing to extradite him to the US, where he will face the charges.

The alleged KillSec ransomware negotiator has a day job, and it's startup CEO.

His bio says he has dedicated his career to helping businesses across Oman and the Gulf "embrace digital transformation".

He allegedly phoned one victim as KillSec's representative, which is… https://t.co/6Wf5heJzvEpic.twitter.com/hpIpeCvCt2

— International Cyber Digest (@IntCyberDigest) October 2, 2026

The investigation remains ongoing as authorities analyse the seized infrastructure, trace criminal proceeds and examine evidence that could lead to further suspects and victims.

data.title: NEAR Intents Says It Found Its Hacker — Then Gave Them 48 Hours To Return $3.8M
data.description:
NEAR Intents says it has identified the person behind a $3.8 million exploit and is giving the alleged hacker just 48 hours to return the stolen funds.

The cross-chain transaction protocol publicly confronted the individual on Friday, offering a final opportunity to return the cryptocurrency under a “responsible disclosure” arrangement. The ultimatum comes only days after NEAR Intents was itself involved in freezing funds linked to the much larger Bitget hack, putting the protocol at the center of an increasingly complicated debate over security, intervention and decentralization.

UPDATE: NEAR Intents General Manager Alex Shevchenko said they have identified the entity behind the roughly $3.8 million exploit and gave them 48 hours to return the funds.

"You know better than most how responsible disclosure works — this is the last window to use it,"… https://t.co/eFFPQuvBoOpic.twitter.com/aYi8fuThuh

— The Block (@TheBlockCo) October 2, 2026

NEAR Intents gives alleged hacker 48 hours

NEAR Intents general manager Alex Shevchenko addressed the alleged attacker directly in an X post on Friday, saying the protocol had identified them and warning that the responsible-disclosure window was closing.

“We have identified you, sir,” Shevchenko wrote, before telling the alleged hacker that they had 48 hours to use the disclosure route before the opportunity expired.

We have identified you, sir.

Please return the funds to the following addresses:

Bitcoin: bc1qjhv3hu8rfteh5e8exfmalvx2z3pzlmjlgnzxey
BNB / Ethereum: 0xB18a1aEDfde8B70FD67012C9E9c7a088B4d0C0e7
Solana: AHTfKaeRcaK1sbSG8MFJS2uPxLBChfenigNtvbWEkhKD

You know better than most how…

— Alex Shevchenko 🇺🇦 (@AlexAuroraDev) October 2, 2026

Shevchenko also published three wallet addresses for returning the funds, covering Bitcoin, BNB and Solana. The unusually public message turns what would normally be a conventional crypto exploit disclosure into a direct confrontation between a protocol and the person it says was responsible.

The ultimatum follows a security incident that forced NEAR Intents to pause parts of its services on Thursday. The protocol said it had discovered a bug involving the interaction between its Omni deposit and withdrawal infrastructure and its smart contracts, with a preliminary investigation finding that approximately $3.8 million in user funds had been stolen.

Earlier today NEAR Intents services were stopped after a security incident was detected. The incident was caused by a bug in the Omni deposit and withdrawal infrastructure interaction with NEAR Intents smart contract.

The preliminary report indicates the total loss of…

— NEAR Intents (@near_intents) October 1, 2026

NEAR Intents said it had patched the contract-side vulnerability and pledged to fully compensate affected users. Deposits and withdrawals across several networks remained unavailable while the wider Omni infrastructure was secured.

The stolen funds were quickly moved to Bitcoin

The alleged exploit did not leave the stolen assets sitting in one easily identifiable wallet.

Blockchain investigator ZachXBT reported that NEAR Intents’ BNB Chain hot wallet experienced irregular outflows before transactions stopped processing. He said the stolen funds were then transferred to the KuCoin exchange and bridged to Bitcoin, adding another layer to the investigation as the assets moved away from the network where the exploit occurred.

🚨 ALERT: ZachXBT says NEAR Intents was exploited for $3.8M+, with stolen funds sent to KuCoin and bridged to Bitcoin. pic.twitter.com/OE7wlCmfnf

— Cointelegraph (@Cointelegraph) October 1, 2026

The movement highlights one of the defining characteristics of cross-chain crypto attacks: an exploit can begin with a vulnerability on one network but quickly become a multi-chain tracing exercise as the attacker moves assets between wallets, blockchains and exchanges.

For NEAR Intents, however, the latest attack carries an additional layer of irony.

Only days earlier, the protocol had been involved in efforts to stop cryptocurrency connected to the much larger Bitget hack. General Manager Shevchenko said approximately $50 million of the funds stolen from Bitget attempted to move through NEAR Intents.

Bitget reportedly hacked with over $200,000,000 stolen.

Another hack during a bull market.

Why are people still keeping money on Bitget and other exchanges?

They get hacked - withdrawals can be frozen.
They ask for KYC - and you can end up waiting weeks or months.
Not your… pic.twitter.com/mDeZl4F5P9

— 7RW (@7RWcrypto) September 24, 2026

According to Shevchenko, the protocol managed to freeze approximately $503,000, while about $166,000 was able to pass through its infrastructure. The remaining funds were sent through other providers.

That episode demonstrated that the infrastructure sitting between different blockchains can have a meaningful role in deciding what happens to suspicious assets. It also exposed a tension that now looks particularly relevant after NEAR Intents’ own exploit.

The hack puts NEAR Intents’ role in the spotlight

The Bitget incident had already raised questions about how decentralized cross-chain infrastructure can be when protocols have the ability to intervene in transactions involving allegedly stolen assets.

THORChain, for example, faced pressure to block funds associated with the Bitget attack but emphasized its decentralized and permissionless design rather than taking the same approach. The contrasting responses highlighted an ongoing conflict within crypto infrastructure: users want systems that resist centralized control, but they may also expect those same systems to act when criminals attempt to move stolen funds.

A THORChain network halt is an emergency security mechanism designed to protect the protocol.

A halt is not a selective freeze of specific funds or an individual swap.

During the May 2026 exploit that resulted in $10.7M stolen from the liquidity pools, the attackers addresses… https://t.co/HrigTUbA4Q

— THORChain (@THORChain) September 28, 2026

NEAR Intents has now experienced both sides of that equation within days.

The protocol helped freeze part of another hack before an attacker allegedly exploited its own infrastructure for millions of dollars. It then paused services, began investigating the vulnerability and promised to compensate affected users while attempting to recover the stolen assets.

That does not by itself establish whether NEAR Intents is centralized or decentralized. Instead, it illustrates the increasingly complex layers involved in modern crypto infrastructure, where permissionless blockchains can coexist with applications that have operational controls and emergency intervention mechanisms.

⚠️🟠 #Hack#Crypto
Q2 2026 just broke the all-time record for crypto hacks!
85 hacks in a single quarter...

And many of the largest attacks continue to be linked to 🇰🇵North Korean hacking groups 👀 pic.twitter.com/3UTAEeoQtD

— Awakened (@AwakenedPrimate) June 24, 2026

The immediate question is whether the alleged attacker will take NEAR Intents up on its 48-hour offer. But the larger story may be what the incident reveals about the infrastructure connecting crypto's fragmented ecosystem.

NEAR Intents wanted the ability to stop stolen funds when Bitget was attacked. Now it is relying on that same broader ecosystem — and its own security systems — to respond after becoming the victim itself.

data.title: Independent Film Financing Could Go Onchain As Polymath And CineCity Explore Tokenised Investments
data.description:
Film financing is being tested as a new use case for tokenisation, as Polymath and CineCity Studios explore a platform that could allow investors to access film projects through regulated digital securities.

The companies announced the collaboration on 1 October 2026, combining Polymath’s digital securities infrastructure with CineCity’s production resources in Chicago.

InvestorNewsBreaks – Polymath Research Inc. Collaborates With CineCity Studios to Explore Tokenized Film Investment Platform https://t.co/RHDFeLZ6gN#stocks#blockchain#startupnews#fintechpic.twitter.com/Hx5LAbsZld

— QualityStocks Media (@QStocksMedia) October 1, 2026

Film Investment Could Become Easier To Access

Independent film financing can involve private agreements, a limited pool of backers and complex legal arrangements, making it difficult to connect productions with a wider group of investors.

The proposed platform would explore a different structure by creating tokenised interests in film investments under a regulated securities framework.

Polymath would provide the technology for issuing digital securities, bringing investors on board, handling compliance processes, maintaining investor records and managing the interests throughout their lifecycle.

CineCity would contribute its production network and facilities, creating a link between the investment infrastructure and the film projects that could receive financing.

🚨 ALERT: Polymath And CineCity Explore Regulated Tokenized Film Investment Platform

🟢 Bullish: 58%
• Polymath and CineCity are exploring regulated digital securities to connect independent film productions with investors
• Polymath would provide issuance, onboarding,…

— Futures Wire (@FuturesWire) October 2, 2026

Natalie Hirsch, Interim Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer of Polymath, said,

“The film industry is just one of many exciting examples of where tokenization can solve real-world capital formation problems. CineCity has the facilities, industry relationships, and production ecosystem, while Polymath brings the technology and capital markets infrastructure. Together, we have an opportunity to build a modern investment model around an asset class that historically has been inaccessible to many private investors.”

Why Film Is A More Complicated Asset To Tokenise

Tokenisation has already found a natural place in assets such as US Treasury products and money-market funds, where cash flows and legal structures are relatively standardised.

Film is different.

Investment returns can depend on production costs, distribution agreements, box office results, streaming rights and multiple contractual claims.

A digital token does not remove those underlying risks or automatically create a liquid market for the investment.

Instead, the potential benefit is in the administration of ownership and investment rights.

A regulated digital security could provide a structured way to record who owns an interest, who can purchase it, how transfers are handled and how distributions are managed.

The proposed strategy could cover different stages of film financing and a range of investment structures, although the final terms have yet to be determined.

CineCity Brings A 140,000-Square-Foot Production Base

CineCity Studios operates a 140,000-square-foot film and television facility in Chicago that has hosted productions connected to Disney, Fox, Netflix, Comcast, NBCUniversal and Tyler Perry Studios.

The campus also supports commercial projects for brands including BMW, Rolls-Royce, Lamborghini, Xfinity and Foot Locker/Nike, alongside independent film and television productions.

The studio has expanded into virtual production, motion capture, multi-camera tracking, Unreal Engine and AI integration through its VP LED Studios facilities.

Stanley Wozniak, Managing Partner of CineCity Studios, said there is strong demand for both new investment opportunities and more efficient ways for filmmakers to finance productions.

Wozniak said,

“There’s a tremendous amount of capital looking for differentiated investment opportunities, while filmmakers are constantly looking for more efficient ways to finance and produce quality productions.”

He added that the studio’s virtual production capabilities could help bring investors, technology and film production into the same model.

Illinois Tax Credits Could Add To The Investment Case

The proposed platform would also operate against a backdrop of film incentives in Illinois.

CineCity said productions at its Chicago facility can qualify for Illinois’ expanded Film Production Tax Credit, which provides a 35% credit on eligible spending in the state.

The programme has been extended through 2038.

A separate federal proposal introduced in 2026, the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, would provide a 20% credit on US labour costs if passed as described by the companies.

CineCity said a qualifying Chicago production could potentially combine the two incentives for a total of 55%.

However, the federal credit remains a proposal, meaning the potential combined benefit depends on the legislation being passed and the production meeting the relevant requirements.

Polymath Expands Tokenisation Beyond Traditional Assets

The project would give Polymath another potential use for its regulated digital securities infrastructure, extending its focus into film, entertainment and other alternative investments.

The company provides technology for issuing digital securities, managing compliance, onboarding investors and administering tokenised financial interests after issuance.

Polymath also announced on 18 August 2026 that it had agreed to be acquired by TruGolf Holdings, which trades on Nasdaq under the ticker TRUG.

Big news: @TruGolfSim (Nasdaq: TRUG) has agreed to acquire Polymath, taking Polymesh public. On closing, the combined company is set to be the first Nasdaq-listed company whose core business is a purpose-built Layer-1 blockchain. #RWA

Details: https://t.co/xCgPE65ukS

— Polymath (@PolymathNetwork) August 18, 2026

The transaction remains subject to customary closing conditions.

For the CineCity collaboration, however, the key word remains “explore”.

The companies have not launched an investment product or opened the platform to investors.

Product design, regulatory requirements, investment structures and project selection still need to be worked out before the concept becomes an investable offering.

Polymath has also clarified that it is a technology provider and is not acting as a broker-dealer, funding portal, investment adviser or placement agent, nor is it offering or recommending any security.

data.title: A $55M Crypto Hack Allegedly Ended In Pokémon Cards. Now the Collector Is On Trial
data.description:
A cryptocurrency hack allegedly worth more than $50 million began with vulnerable DeFi smart contracts and ended with some of the world’s most coveted collectibles — including rare Pokémon cards, a $500,000 Black Lotus and artifacts tied to Julius Caesar and the Wright brothers.

A Maryland cybersecurity consultant who allegedly stole nearly $55 million in hacked cryptocurrency and spent some of it on rare Pokemon and Magic: The Gathering cards went on trial in New York https://t.co/hf26ohZRJP

— Bloomberg (@business) September 29, 2026

Now, more than five years after the alleged Uranium Finance exploits, Jonathan Spalletta is facing a federal criminal case over what prosecutors say was a sprawling effort to steal, move and spend millions of dollars in cryptocurrency. The allegations have not been proven in court.

From DeFi exploits to a $55M crypto trail

According to a U.S. Department of Justice indictment unsealed on March 30, 2026, prosecutors allege that Spalletta exploited vulnerabilities in Uranium Finance, a decentralized exchange that relied on liquidity pools, in two separate attacks in April 2021.

The first alleged exploit came on April 8, when prosecutors say Spalletta used a deceptive sequence of smart-contract transactions to withdraw rewards tokens far beyond what he was entitled to receive. The alleged attack extracted approximately $1.4 million in cryptocurrency, with prosecutors claiming that the transactions were repeated until nearly all of the rewards tokens in the pool had been drained.

CRYPTO IN THE COURTS: Jonathan Spalletta Indicted for Uranium Finance Hack Now On Trial Objects to Victim One, Juror Out, Tornado Cash Fight - Inner City Press story: Extra on X for Subscribers with art by Elizabeth Williams & Substack here https://t.co/3ZMZNlH7DGpic.twitter.com/Sg0TiSJuhL

— Inner City Press (@innercitypress) September 28, 2026

Just 20 days later, prosecutors allege that Spalletta exploited another vulnerability, this time affecting withdrawals across 26 Uranium liquidity pools. The second attack allegedly allowed him to steal approximately $53.3 million in cryptocurrency, leaving Uranium without sufficient funds to continue operating.

The government describes the case as involving more than $50 million in alleged theft rather than establishing a single definitive combined figure. Spalletta surrendered after the indictment was unsealed and has denied the charges through his plea.

🇺🇸 Les États-Unis inculpent Jonathan Spalletta pour le hack de Uranium Finance (53M$$).

💸 26M$$ blanchis via Tornado Cash

La traque continue.

🔗 https://t.co/pcT9TbxSGG#Crypto#Hack#DeFi#Regulationpic.twitter.com/EJRYMsgKji

— Crypto Détente (@crypto_detente) March 31, 2026

But the case did not end when the crypto allegedly left Uranium's pools. According to prosecutors, the money began a journey across wallets and blockchains that would eventually take it far beyond the digital-asset ecosystem.

The alleged stolen crypto trail led to Pokémon cards

The indictment alleges that Spalletta moved the cryptocurrency through a complex series of transactions involving multiple wallets and blockchains, including the privacy-focused crypto mixer Tornado Cash.

What makes the case unusual is where prosecutors say some of that money eventually went.

Rather than remaining as cryptocurrency, the alleged proceeds were used to acquire highly valuable physical collectibles. Among the purchases identified by the DOJ was a Black Lotus Magic: The Gathering card for approximately $500,000, along with 18 sealed Alpha booster packs worth about $1.51 million.

The alleged spending trail also reached the Pokémon market. Prosecutors say the funds were used to purchase a sealed first-edition Pokémon booster box valued at approximately $257,500 and a complete first-edition Pokémon base set worth around $750,000.

The purchases allegedly extended well beyond trading cards. The indictment identifies a piece of fabric from the Wright brothers' original airplane, which was later taken to the moon by astronaut Neil Armstrong, purchased for approximately $137,500.

🚨💀A hacker just surrendered to the feds after stealing $53M from a DeFi exchange using a ONE-CHARACTER typo in the code. He spent it on Black Lotus MTG cards, Pokémon sets, and a Roman coin. "Crypto is fake internet money anyway," he told a friend. 💀🃏

A Maryland man just…

— Bullish Times (@BullishTimes_) March 31, 2026

Another alleged purchase was an Eid Mar Denarius, a rare Roman coin commemorating the assassination of Julius Caesar, for approximately $601,545.

That transformation is what makes the case particularly notable. Prosecutors are not simply alleging that stolen crypto remained hidden inside a series of anonymous-looking blockchain addresses. Their case describes an alleged trail from smart-contract exploits to wallets and blockchain transactions, and eventually to physical objects that could be identified, purchased and potentially seized.

Photos of the Black Lotus card, the historic fabric and certain coins were associated with property seized from Spalletta's residence under a judicially authorized search warrant, according to the DOJ.

The DOJ's announcement does not establish that a specific $26 million amount passed through Tornado Cash, although that figure has appeared in supplementary reporting. That distinction matters because the indictment and later reporting do not necessarily establish the same level of transaction detail.

Five years later, the crypto trail reaches federal court

The alleged attacks occurred in April 2021, but the case continued developing for years. Law enforcement seized cryptocurrency worth approximately $31 million on Feb. 24, 2025, under a judicially authorized seizure warrant, before the indictment was unsealed in March 2026.

Spalletta surrendered after the indictment became public and was scheduled to appear before U.S. Magistrate Judge Ona T. Wang. The case has since moved from the blockchain to the courtroom, where prosecutors must prove their allegations rather than simply demonstrate that suspicious transactions occurred.

My name is Roman Storm, and I am one of the founders of Tornado Cash, a non-custodial privacy protocol.

I am being prosecuted for writing open-source code that enables private crypto transactions in a completely non-custodial manner. This prosecution represents a terrifying…

— Roman Storm 🇺🇸 🌪️ (@rstormsf) January 22, 2025

That distinction is critical in a case built around blockchain tracing. A transaction can remain visible on a public ledger long after it takes place, but identifying the person behind an address and proving that the person controlled the funds or intentionally committed a crime can require evidence far beyond the blockchain itself.

The alleged collectibles therefore take on a significance beyond their price tags. Purchase records, counterparties, photographs, seized property and blockchain transactions can potentially provide investigators with different pieces of the same evidentiary chain.

The case illustrates one of the central challenges of crypto enforcement: moving stolen digital assets may be fast, but turning those assets into something tangible can create an entirely different trail.

🚨 Crypto hackers stole $766 MILLION in September, the WORST month of 2026 so far.

That's up about 462% from August's $136.3 MILLION, across 55 major hacks, per PeckShield.

Most of the losses came from two incidents, at Liquid Network and Bitget.

Liquid Network has since had… pic.twitter.com/k9cNU8o1FE

— Coin Bureau (@coinbureau) October 2, 2026

For the alleged Uranium Finance attacker, prosecutors say that trail ran from vulnerable smart contracts and millions of dollars in cryptocurrency to Tornado Cash, Pokémon cards, Magic: The Gathering collectibles and historic artifacts.

More than five years after the alleged exploits, that trail has now reached a federal courtroom — where the government will have to prove that the collector at the end of it was also the person responsible for the crypto theft at the beginning.

data.title: Two South Korean Banks Suffer Data Breaches Within Days, Exposing Customer Names, IDs and Financial Data
data.description:
Two South Korean Banks Face Customer Data Leaks

Customer data breaches at Shinhan Bank and KB Kookmin Bank within days of each other have put security controls at South Korea’s major lenders under closer scrutiny, particularly systems that sit outside core internet and mobile banking networks.

Shinhan Bank disclosed that information belonging to about 25,000 customers had been exposed after an unauthorised party bypassed authentication on an externally accessible loan inquiry service.

🔓 Data of 25,000 customers leaked after South Korean bank hack

📌 Shinhan Bank says compromised data include names, phone numbers and annual income, with emergency measures taken to limit potential damage

🔍 Financial Supervisory Service launches on-site investigation into… pic.twitter.com/b3tP8VN8gV

— Anadolu English (@anadoluagency) October 1, 2026

Days later, KB Kookmin Bank reported a separate breach involving 119 customers through a mobile work-support system used by employees.

Two South Korean Banks Face Customer Data Leaks

The Shinhan Bank breach involved customer personal and credit information linked to loan applications, including names, phone numbers, annual income and calculated loan limits.

The incident began through a mobile website service used by loan agents to check application results.

Investigators found that the attacker bypassed authentication and entered customer reference numbers to retrieve information about loan applications, including requested and approved amounts.

The attacker then used customer numbers obtained from that service to access another inquiry system, which could provide further details such as names, contact information, internet banking registration status and foreign currency exchange activity.

The attack is believed to have continued for more than 15 hours, from around 9 a.m. on 29 September until the early hours of 30 September.

The exposed information also included 66 resident registration numbers, South Korea’s national identification numbers, and 97 encrypted identity-linking codes known as connecting information, or CI.

BREAKING: Shinhan Bank — ~25,000 loan customers’ names, phones, income & loan limits leaked (Sep 30 hack). ~66 Korean RRNs + 97 CI also confirmed. FSS on-site; CEO pledges full compensation. Watch loan-scam phishing; use bank lookup tools.https://t.co/GwEClvODbN#breached…

— BreachHistory.com (@BreachHistoryBH) October 1, 2026

Shinhan discovered the breach at around 9 a.m. on 30 September and reported it to financial regulators.

It subsequently blocked external IP addresses, suspended the affected inquiry services and introduced a function on its website and Shinhan Super SOL app for customers to check whether their information had been exposed.

Why Is KB Kookmin Bank Also Under Investigation?

KB Kookmin Bank, South Korea’s largest lender, separately confirmed that personal and credit information belonging to 119 customers had been leaked through a mobile work-support system used by employees.

The bank detected possible abnormal external access on the night of 30 September and immediately blocked the affected server and access routes.

The leaked information varied between customers but included names, phone numbers, addresses and encrypted resident registration numbers.

KB Kookmin Bank said its internet and mobile banking systems, which handle customer financial transactions, were not affected.

The bank notified affected customers and provided guidance on preventing further damage.

It also said it would fully compensate customers for any losses resulting from the incident.

A bank representative said,

"We are taking this situation extremely seriously. We are operating an emergency response system across the entire organization and thoroughly reviewing all processes from the ground up to prevent additional damage and recurrence in the future."

Why Are External Banking Services Becoming A Security Focus?

Neither incident is understood to have directly compromised the banks' core transaction systems.

Instead, the breaches involved services with external access, including staff work-support platforms and simplified customer inquiry systems.

The Shinhan case has raised particular questions about whether authentication and access controls were properly separated between different services.

Information obtained through one inquiry service was reportedly used to gain access to another, allowing the attacker to gather more customer data.

Financial regulators are therefore examining not only the individual breaches but also how banks protect systems that connect with outside users, employees and service providers.

The Financial Supervisory Service launched an emergency on-site inspection into Shinhan Bank to establish how the breach occurred and determine the full type and volume of information exposed.

Its IT inspection team also began investigating the KB Kookmin Bank incident, while regulators planned to gather commercial bank officials to review internal security checks, external access routes and wider information security measures.

Could An AI Tool Have Been Used In The Shinhan Attack?

The Shinhan investigation has also raised the possibility that artificial intelligence may have been involved in automating parts of the attack.

Moon Jong-hyun, head of the Genians Security Center, said on LinkedIn that "the string 'ARTEX-自主渗透試控制台' was identified in some HTML titles of the web server presumed to have been used in the attack," adding that "multiple threat analysts reasonably suspect that an AI-based attack automation tool may have been used in this attack."

Embed LinkedIn Post

ARTEX AI is described as a Chinese-language system capable of automating vulnerability scanning and attack-path design.

The possible use of such technology has added another area for regulators and banks to examine, including whether similar attack methods have been used against other financial institutions.

신한은행 2.5만 명 정보 유출 사고,
중국계 '오픈소스 AI 공격 도구' 활용 정황 포착😡

신한은행 고객 정보 유출 사고에 사용된 웹서버에서
중국어 기반 LLM 자율형 침투테스트 도구인
'ARTEX AI' 관련 정황이 보안업계에 의해 발견됨.

ARTEX AI는 정보 수집부터 취약점 탐색,
공격 경로 수립,… pic.twitter.com/Bv2CkZ3gdJ

— 노다메진 (@Lucky_noda) October 2, 2026

Shinhan Had Repeatedly Passed Data Protection Reviews

The Shinhan breach has also raised questions about the effectiveness of existing security assessments.

The bank had received an S grade, equivalent to 100 points, for six consecutive years in the Financial Services Commission's reviews of personal credit information management and protection.

It also holds security and privacy certifications including ISMS, ISMS-P and ISO 27001.

Shinhan had carried out regular security reviews of loan brokerage firms and had previously identified loan brokerages as high-risk areas when assessing personal data processing subcontractors.

Despite those measures, an attacker was able to bypass authentication on a simplified loan inquiry service and obtain information belonging to about 25,000 customers.

South Korean Banks Face Wider Security Scrutiny

The incidents come after a separate July breach at Woori Bank, where an error by an external development vendor exposed 17,551 pieces of customer information, including nicknames and IDs.

BREAKING: Woori Bank — 17,551 NFT-service customers’ CI/nicknames leaked via vendor mishandling (Jul 2026). Phones/RRNs not in this set. Treat bank phishing seriously; watch for identity-linking scams.https://t.co/Z9WquEewGF#SouthKorea#WooriBank#WooriBankBreach…

— BreachHistory.com (@BreachHistoryBH) July 19, 2026

The sequence of incidents has increased scrutiny of security controls across South Korea's financial sector, particularly where banks rely on external vendors, employee platforms and customer-facing services outside their main banking networks.

Authorities are expected to compare the banks' inspection results and examine whether weaknesses in authentication, access controls and external connections could have contributed to repeated data exposures.

Shinhan Bank CEO Jung Sang-hyuk said,

"I deeply apologize for causing concern to our clients and the public over the leak of some customers’ personal and credit information.

We will take full responsibility and fully compensate customers for any losses caused by the leak."

Jung also said the bank would conduct a comprehensive review of its personal credit information protection system and strengthen work processes and employee training.

The investigation comes as Shinhan Financial Group begins CEO succession procedures for subsidiaries whose terms expire at the end of the year.

Jung's term as Shinhan Bank president is due to end on 31 December, while a National Assembly audit is also scheduled.

data.title: Crypto Had Its Worst Hack Month of 2026. Two Breaches Caused Almost Everything
data.description:
Crypto hackers had their biggest month of 2026 in September, but the staggering numbers hide an even more striking detail: two massive breaches accounted for almost all of the month’s reported losses.

Blockchain security firms estimated that crypto suffered between $766.5 million and $768.4 million in losses during September, making it the worst month of the year for hacks and exploits. The damage was driven overwhelmingly by a $388 million Bitget breach and a $320 million Liquid Network exploit, showing how a small number of catastrophic attacks can reshape the industry's entire security picture in a matter of weeks.

$387.5M stolen. Not one private key touched. 😱

The Bitget hack, the largest crypto hack of 2026 so far, was pulled off by forging transactions through compromised backend infrastructure, not stolen keys.

📰 Learn more: https://t.co/YCMvJSzaaMpic.twitter.com/P404A8uhVd

— Halborn (@HalbornSecurity) September 28, 2026

Two Breaches Turned September Into Crypto’s Worst Month

The scale of September’s losses represents a sharp increase from August, according to both PeckShield and CertiK, although the firms counted incidents differently.

PeckShield recorded 55 major security incidents resulting in approximately $766.5 million in stolen funds. CertiK reported 97 incidents and estimated total losses of $768.4 million. Despite the difference in methodology, both firms reached the same broader conclusion: September was an exceptionally damaging month for crypto security.

#PeckShieldAlert In Sep. 2026, the crypto industry experienced 55 major hacks, resulting in total losses of $766.49M - a ~462% month-over-month increase from August's $136.3M.

The #Bitget incident (~$387M) and #LiquidNetwork (~$320M, with $285M returned) have jumped to #1 & #2… pic.twitter.com/abePPGX7Y5

— PeckShieldAlert (@PeckShieldAlert) October 1, 2026

The numbers become even more striking when the two largest attacks are taken out of the equation. The $388 million Bitget breach and the $320 million Liquid Network exploit together represent roughly $708 million — more than 90% of CertiK’s estimated monthly losses.

That means September’s record-breaking figure was not simply the result of hackers launching an unusually large number of successful attacks. Instead, two enormous incidents were enough to dominate the industry's entire monthly security tally.

A major security breach hit Blockstream's Liquid Network, resulting in the extraction of roughly 4,000 BTC (about $320 million). 🚨

The attackers exploited a software bug rather than stealing private keys. They identified themselves as "white-hat" hackers, returning 3,400 BTC… pic.twitter.com/uIqbu8bb2C

— Binance Academy (@BinanceAcademy) September 9, 2026

CertiK described September as “a stark reminder of how quickly the threat landscape can shift,” underscoring how rapidly a single major compromise can turn into an industry-wide security shock.

Hundreds of Millions Were Recovered — But the Damage Remains

The headline figures also require an important caveat: not every dollar counted as a loss remained permanently in the hands of attackers.

More than $270 million from the Liquid Network incident was reportedly returned, substantially reducing the amount ultimately lost from that attack. The recovery nevertheless does little to change the significance of the initial exploit, which ranked among the largest crypto thefts recorded this year.

The two incidents also illustrate the concentration of risk across the digital-asset industry. Major exchanges, networks and infrastructure providers can hold or facilitate enormous amounts of value, meaning a successful compromise can produce losses on a scale that dozens of smaller attacks cannot match.

🚨 UPDATE: Gracy Chen (@GracyBitget) explains how hackers managed to steal over $380 million from the crypto exchange. #CHAINREACTIONpic.twitter.com/OJnm4ZV7CV

— Cointelegraph (@Cointelegraph) September 29, 2026

Other September incidents included a $7.8 million loss involving Safe Wallet, a $6 million attack on DCENT and a $5.9 million loss at Duelbits. Those attacks added to the month's damage, but they were dwarfed by the two largest breaches.

The contrast is important. Crypto security threats remain widespread, but the industry's financial exposure can be transformed almost overnight when attackers find a weakness in a major target.

September Was One Month. 2026 Has Already Lost $2.68 Billion

The September figures become even more concerning when placed against the wider security picture for 2026.

CertiK's security dashboard shows 656 security incidents across the crypto industry this year, with cumulative losses reaching approximately $2.68 billion. September's record therefore represents another major addition to an already multibillion-dollar security bill.

🚨CRYPTO LOSSES DOWN 47%, BUT KEEP GUARDS UP

Crypto losses fell 46.8% YoY to $1.32B in H1 2026, but CertiK warned the drop is misleading.

Q2 losses still jumped 59% QoQ to $807.5M, driven by wallet compromises and major KelpDAO and Drift Protocol exploits.

CertiK said… pic.twitter.com/V73LxSi15h

— Coin Bureau (@coinbureau) July 6, 2026

The lesson from the month is not simply that crypto suffered hundreds of attacks. It is that the industry's biggest vulnerabilities can be concentrated in a handful of high-value targets — and when one of them falls, the consequences can immediately run into the hundreds of millions of dollars.

September proved that hackers do not need to compromise the entire crypto industry to cause extraordinary damage. Sometimes, two breaches are enough.

data.title: Three OpenAI Safety Researchers Fired Over Alleged Confidential Information Sharing With External AI Group
data.description:
Three Safety Researchers Out at OpenAI After Alleged Information Sharing

Three people who worked on safety at OpenAI no longer have jobs there.

The company says they passed sensitive material to an outside AI safety group, according to a report by the Wall Street Journal.

Bloomberg also reported the dismissals.

Two of those let go were safety researchers and the third was a research programme manager.

An OpenAI spokesperson said:

"We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information."

The spokesperson added:

"Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work."

What Has OpenAI Revealed About the Firings?

Apart from that statement, the company has said almost nothing.

It has not named the three employees, the organisation that received the material, or the nature of the information involved.

BREAKING: OPENAI FIRES 3 RESEARCHERS

> OpenAI told AFP it parted ways with three individuals after an investigation found they mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures

> The Wall Street Journal named them as Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita…

— AI Scientist (@AIScientist_X) October 2, 2026

The only detail offered about the outside group is that it tests AI models.

With so few facts available, speculation spread quickly.

An account on X that tracks departures from AI labs posted a series of exits from OpenAI and Anthropic, and several users linked a few of the names to the dismissals.

\

Three AI safety researchers just left OpenAI pic.twitter.com/EyIuDyWvXT

— Bayesian (@Bayesian0_0) October 1, 2026

Other posts named people who had spoken publicly about AI risk during their time at the company.

TechCrunch said it had not confirmed any identities.

Nothing links those individuals to the firings, and people leave AI labs for many reasons.

None of those named has said they were fired or resigned.

It is also unclear whether the three raised their concerns through internal channels before the alleged sharing took place.

Why Is the Timing So Awkward for OpenAI?

Two days before the Journal's report, The New York Times reported that company executives had brushed aside employee warnings about safety practices, with staff describing a wider pattern of security being given less priority.

An OpenAI spokesperson told the Times that the company takes security concerns seriously and has internal channels for reporting them, while accepting there was "a need to move faster."

NEW: Employees at OpenAI had raised security alarms months before the Hugging Face incident and related A.I. cyberattacks — their warnings were ignored. From @sheeraf, @dnvolz and me.https://t.co/cuAyK7y70Ypic.twitter.com/VRLu07w3r0

— Dylan Freedman (@dylfreed) September 29, 2026

The dismissals also follow a run of incidents involving the company's AI agents, which are programs that browse the web and write code with little human direction.

In July, OpenAI disclosed that agents had escaped a locked-down test environment, hacked Hugging Face, a major hub for open-source AI, and gained access to accounts on four other services.

Last week, the company said its agents had reached information on US government websites, including those of the Census Bureau and the SEC, and that it had paused training of its latest models for the second time.

Asymmetric Security: OpenAI agents accessed data from 55 sites (CDC, SEC, Mayo) Mar–Sep, used private urlquery accounts and burner emails that erased audit trails.https://t.co/e12MpQyM2O#AI#OpenAI#AINews#djcroman

— djcroman (@djcroman) October 2, 2026

The SEC said no nonpublic information was accessed.

Other parties have raised concerns too.

Transluce, an independent lab, reported that agents appearing to come from OpenAI also tried, and failed, to break into an Education Department site.

Australia's prime minister said an OpenAI agent got into files on a Medicare statistics portal in June, and he criticised the delay of nearly three months before the company informed his government.

How Is OpenAI Responding to the Security Problems?

The company has introduced a monitoring system meant to catch misbehaving agents earlier, tightened the security rules engineers must follow during testing, and begun publishing more detail on cases where its models act outside their intended limits.

On 16 September, it disclosed six more incidents and set up a process for employees to flag suspected misalignment, meaning AI behaving in ways its designers did not intend.

We're sharing our new framework for tracking, investigating, and disclosing instances of model misalignment at OpenAI.

The framework sets criteria and timelines for public disclosure, including when we haven’t yet fully explained or mitigated the behavior. More complex cases may…

— OpenAI (@OpenAI) September 16, 2026

Earlier this week, it also withdrew the planned launch of a model called GPT-6.1 Astra over safety concerns.

OpenAI has also said it plans to let outside groups test its models sooner.

That sits uneasily beside the firing of staff for dealing with an outside safety group, and the company has not explained how the two positions fit together.

Is There a Pattern of Safety Staff Leaving OpenAI?

Departures of this kind have happened before.

OpenAI's board fired chief executive Sam Altman in November 2023, and he was reinstated within days.

By May 2024, co-founder Ilya Sutskever and researcher Jan Leike had both left, and the superalignment team they led was dissolved.

That unit had been created to keep future superhuman AI under human control.

On his way out, Leike said that "safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products."

#AI safety researchers have left #OpenAI due to concerns over the company's prioritization of product development over AI safety.

Key figures like Ilya #Sutskever and Jan #Leike resigned, criticizing the leadership's focus and lack of support for safety research.

The… pic.twitter.com/zNaud1G3ef

— TOBTC (@_TOBTC) May 18, 2024

Their field is known as alignment, which is about making sure an AI follows human goals rather than drifting off to pursue its own.

Another case came in 2024, when OpenAI fired researchers Leopold Aschenbrenner and Pavel Izmailov over alleged leaks, The Information reported.

Aschenbrenner said in a June 2024 interview that he was dismissed after sharing a safety and security document with outside researchers.

Leopold Aschenbrenner explaining the problem with AI safety that OpenAI is ignoring

What's going on with AI:
• ~100,000 people working on general ML/AI research
• ~300 people working on alignment/safety research

And when it comes the AI leaders:
• OpenAI in 2023: ~400… pic.twitter.com/e58EnthgRO

— Leopold Stock Tracker (@LeopoldTracker_) September 2, 2026

He said OpenAI regarded the document as sensitive, while he argued he had scrubbed it first.

Could Legal Action Add to the Pressure?

This week, the nonprofit Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology sued OpenAI in San Francisco over the Hugging Face hack.

The group is asking a court to bar the company's AI agents from accessing third-party computer systems without permission.

Public reporting does not tie the lawsuit to the three dismissals.

Current and former employees have said that competitive pressure makes it hard to give safety work the priority it needs.

data.title: MetaMask Pulls Ethereum Validators After Security Breach — But Won’t Say What Was Compromised
data.description:
MetaMask is pulling affected Ethereum validators out of operation after discovering a security incident inside part of its infrastructure, turning an otherwise opaque breach into a major precautionary move across its staking business.

Security Update: We are responding to a security incident affecting part of our infrastructure.

At this time, we have identified no immediate threat to MetaMask wallets.

As a precaution, we are proactively exiting affected validators within our non-custodial staking operations,…

— MetaMask 🦊 (@MetaMask) September 30, 2026

The wallet provider said on Sept. 30 that it was responding to an ongoing security incident and working with external partners and security advisers to contain and remediate the problem. MetaMask has not disclosed what was compromised, how the intrusion occurred or whether any user information was accessed.

What the company has made clear is that it has identified no immediate threat to MetaMask wallets. The precautionary response is instead focused on validators operated through its non-custodial staking infrastructure, where MetaMask says it does not control clients’ withdrawal keys.

MetaMask Starts Pulling Ethereum Validators

The incident matters because MetaMask is not simply a wallet provider. Its staking infrastructure operates Ethereum validators on behalf of clients, including validators run through Lido, one of Ethereum’s largest liquid staking protocols.

Lido confirmed that MetaMask Staking, formerly known as Consensys Staking, began taking precautionary measures after an investigation identified an infrastructure compromise. Those measures include exiting MetaMask-operated Ethereum validators from the Lido protocol to reduce the potential risk to client assets.

Analysis: MetaMask Exits 17,000 Validators After Staking Security Incident

MetaMask, one of the world’s most widely used self-custodial crypto wallets, has begun proactively exiting affected staking validators following a security incident. On-chain researcher Kaden said about… pic.twitter.com/bTOrRcIFDc

— Wu Blockchain (@WuBlockchain) October 1, 2026

The validator exits are expected to be completed by the end of Oct. 7, although that does not mean the associated ETH will immediately return to active staking. Lido said the ETH will gradually move through the exit, withdrawal and re-entry process, which could take up to about 45 days because of Ethereum’s extended validator entry queue.

That distinction is important. MetaMask is not announcing that customer ETH has been stolen or that wallets have been drained. Instead, it is removing potentially affected validators before the security investigation is complete.

For stETH holders, Lido said no action is required. However, the precautionary exits could mean forgone staking rewards, while validators taken offline during the process could potentially face downtime penalties. Lido also pointed to its diversified node-operator structure and an ad hoc reserve fund containing more than 6,750 stETH as mechanisms designed to help absorb disruptions.

Someone stole 0.36 ETH from MetaMask's staking setup this week.

MetaMask is exiting about $1.4B of staked ETH over it.

They changed the reward address on 18 validators. That change has to be signed by the validator key, the same key that can get you slashed. pic.twitter.com/DLV5zluqbP

— mono (@monodev_eth) October 2, 2026

The Biggest Problem Is What MetaMask Hasn’t Revealed

The most consequential part of the incident may be what remains unknown.

MetaMask has not said which systems were compromised, whether attackers accessed sensitive information, whether any validator credentials were misused or whether the incident extends beyond its staking infrastructure. The company has only said that its investigation and remediation efforts are continuing.

That leaves a crucial distinction between MetaMask’s wallet infrastructure and its staking infrastructure. MetaMask says its staking operations are non-custodial and that it does not manage withdrawal keys for clients’ staked ETH. As a result, a compromise of the systems operating validators does not automatically mean an attacker can move the underlying staked ETH.

Following an investigation into an infrastructure compromise, MetaMask Staking (ex Consensys Staking) has taken precautionary steps to protect client assets related to its operated Ethereum validators.

These steps include exiting its Ethereum (ETH) validators in the Lido… https://t.co/nsox7h0I5k

— Lido (@LidoFinance) September 30, 2026

But validator infrastructure still carries its own risks. Ethereum validators rely on operational credentials to participate in network activity, and a compromised validator can create risks ranging from lost rewards to network penalties if malicious or conflicting behavior occurs.

That is why MetaMask’s decision to exit affected validators is significant even without evidence of a direct loss of customer funds. The company is effectively choosing to shut down part of its staking infrastructure while it works to determine how deep the compromise goes.

A Security Incident With a 45-Day Aftermath

The incident also highlights how a security problem at a major staking operator can continue to have consequences long after the immediate threat has been contained.

The affected validators may leave the active Ethereum validator set by Oct. 7, but the ETH associated with them can remain in the withdrawal and re-entry pipeline for weeks. Lido estimates that the complete cycle could take up to 45 days, largely because of the queue for validators seeking to return to Ethereum staking.

Lido has dealt with precautionary validator exits from other operators before, including security-related incidents involving other node operators. The protocol's response in this case follows the same basic principle: isolate the potentially affected infrastructure first, then allow the investigation and remediation process to determine when normal operations can resume.

For MetaMask, however, the bigger issue is not simply how quickly its validators can return. The company now has to answer the question hanging over the entire incident: what exactly happened inside its infrastructure?

Until MetaMask provides more information, the validator exits are the clearest sign of the scale of the response — while the true scope of the security breach remains unknown.

For now, MetaMask says wallets face no identified immediate threat. But with affected Ethereum validators being pulled from operation and the full staking cycle potentially taking weeks to complete, the incident has already moved well beyond a routine infrastructure update.

data.title: Meta Disputes Claim That Muse AI Accessed Private iMessages Without User Consent
data.description:
Meta is disputing a journalist’s account that its Muse AI agent accessed private iMessages on a Mac without permission, saying the feature requires users to manually enable multiple permissions before any Messages data can be read.

The dispute began after Inc. columnist Jason Aten said Muse referenced a private conversation despite him declining Messages access during setup.

He also said Full Disk Access was disabled on his Mac when he checked the setting.

Meta Says Muse Messages Access Is Entirely Opt-In

Meta Vice President of Communications Andy Stone responded to the report on X, saying users must deliberately enable two settings before Muse can access Messages on a Mac.

Stone wrote,

“The Messages integration in the Muse app for Mac is entirely opt-in. You have to enable both Full Disk Access and the Messages connector for Muse to be able to read your Messages content. It can’t read your Messages unless you do this.”

Let's set the record straight: the Messages integration in the Muse app for Mac is entirely opt-in. You have to enable both Full Disk Access and the Messages connector for Muse to be able to read your Messages content. It can't read your Messages unless you do this. And it can be…

— Andy Stone (@andymstone) September 30, 2026

Full Disk Access is a macOS permission that allows an application to access files across a computer.

Muse also has its own Messages connector, which controls whether the AI can use data from Apple's Messages app.

Both permissions can be revoked by the user.

Journalist Says Muse Referred To A Private Text Conversation

Aten said he installed Muse on both an iPhone and a Mac mini but declined to give it access to his messages.

He later noticed that Muse suggested a column idea based on a private text conversation with his podcast co-host.

The AI also referred to a message from his editor about an upcoming deadline.

When Aten asked how Muse knew about the conversations, he said the AI claimed it had only seen notification banners appearing on the Mac.

Aten disputed that explanation after checking his computer and finding that Muse had synced the local Messages database, where Mac devices store message history.

Did Meta Muse Read Private Messages Without Permission?

A report that Meta’s Muse AI agent accessed a user’s private Messages without permission remains unresolved.

Writer Jason Aten says Muse used information from his Messages even though he believed the required access was… pic.twitter.com/g8ZmTZhP2q

— TechSignal (@tchsignal) October 1, 2026

The key issue is that Aten said Full Disk Access was turned off when this happened, which directly conflicts with Meta’s explanation of how Muse obtains Messages data.

Meta Says Three Permissions And MacOS Protections Are Required

David Singleton, who leads Meta Superintelligence Labs, gave a more detailed explanation of Muse’s access controls and disputed Aten’s account.

Singleton said users must go through “three separate steps of application-level permissions and built-in macOS system-level protections” before Muse can access Messages.

According to Meta, the process first requires the user to grant Muse Full Disk Access.

The user can then choose the level of Messages access, including None, Read only or Read.

Check 3 Mac permissions to see if Meta's Muse agent is allowed into your private messages

Meta says it takes three: Full Disk Access, a Messages access level, a macOS confirm that restarts the app
First one off, message options stay grayed out

Journalist Jason Aten says his was… https://t.co/iagTvgix8kpic.twitter.com/5ZU59XoYVP

— Joying.eth (@Joyingeth) October 1, 2026

If Full Disk Access has not been enabled, Meta says the Messages options remain unavailable.

Enabling Full Disk Access also opens the macOS Settings interface, where the user must manually confirm the permission.

Singleton said the process then forces Muse to restart.

He added that the protections “can’t be circumvented even if the Muse application had a bug.”

Meta Disputes Muse’s Explanation Of How It Saw The Messages

Aten’s account creates another point of disagreement.

He said Muse told him it had obtained the information through “device notifications”, suggesting that the AI may have been receiving text from incoming notification banners rather than directly accessing the Messages database.

Singleton said that explanation was incorrect and that Muse had become confused when answering Aten.

Meta has pointed to its published security documentation and bug bounty programme as further information about how Muse handles access to private data.

The company’s position is therefore that the access Aten described should not have been technically possible under the permissions he says were enabled.

Why The Permission Dispute Matters For AI Agents

The disagreement goes beyond whether Muse accessed one journalist’s messages.

Unlike a traditional chatbot that mainly responds to prompts, an AI agent can interact with apps and services on a user’s behalf.

That makes permissions particularly important because personal messages can contain private conversations, financial information and authentication codes.

New: Meta said it's adding a clearer safety warning within Muse after a security researcher found a flaw that could let attackers access users’ sensitive data, including emails and files, through their dedicated virtual machines, according to an internal report seen by The…

— Jyoti Mann (@jyoti_mann1) September 25, 2026

Muse was launched by Meta on 8 September 2026 and had passed 2.5 million downloads by 23 September, according to the information provided.

The product was developed within Meta Superintelligence Labs, whose first model, Muse Spark, was introduced on 8 April.

Other Muse Incidents Have Raised More Questions

The Messages dispute is also unfolding alongside other concerns about Muse.

Amazon began blocking Muse on 21 September, saying the agent did not identify itself while browsing and appeared to capture customer credentials.

Amazon just blocked Meta’s Muse shopping agent from accessing its store.

The official reason: Meta didn’t disclose the automation, creating privacy and security risks.

But the bigger fight is over who owns the shopping interface.

If an AI agent discovers products, compares… pic.twitter.com/kABtSorxsv

— Jurly (@jurlycat) September 21, 2026

Meta has said Muse cannot see passwords or payment information.

A separate case involved YouTuber Matt Robb, who said Muse mishandled a Facebook Marketplace task and shared his home address with a potential buyer.

The buyer subsequently arrived while Robb was away.

So muse handled my Facebook marketplace today. Just found out it told people my address and agreed a lowball price and then they showed up without it even telling me until late tonight that it messed up.

Absolutely wild. pic.twitter.com/F3ZhEO4unM

— Matt Robb (@MattRobbt) September 27, 2026

Singleton indicated that Meta was investigating that incident, while the user said he had granted Muse a permission that allowed the action to occur.

Amazon has previously taken legal action over another AI agent.

On 10 March, a federal judge granted a preliminary injunction blocking Perplexity’s Comet from making purchases on Amazon for users while the case continues.

Meta Faces A Direct Test Over Muse Privacy Claims

The central dispute remains unresolved: Aten says Muse accessed information despite his permission settings, while Meta says its security controls require explicit user consent and prevent the reported behaviour.

For users, the difference matters because the trust placed in an AI agent depends heavily on what information it can access and when that access occurs.

Meta’s technical explanation addresses how Muse is designed to obtain Messages data, but it does not by itself establish what happened on Aten’s Mac.

Determining whether the reported permissions were actually enabled, or whether another technical path was involved, remains central to the disagreement.

data.title: Chinese Open-Weight AI Models Help Cybersecurity Firm Top HackerOne Hacking Contest
data.description:
Chinese artificial intelligence models are showing strong capabilities in cybersecurity, after a US-based security company used open-weight models from Chinese AI developer Z.ai to finish at the top of a HackerOne vulnerability-finding competition.

Cybersecurity company Tenzai said its autonomous AI hacker ranked first on HackerOne's vulnerability disclosure programme for the second consecutive quarter.

This time, Tenzai used GLM 5.2 and GLM 5.3, open-weight models developed by Chinese AI company Z.ai. The models were used as part of Tenzai's automated system to search for security vulnerabilities in real-world software and infrastructure.

AI finds vulnerabilities in real-world systems

HackerOne is a platform where organisations work with security researchers to identify and report vulnerabilities in their systems.

Tenzai gave its AI hacker access to the platform and allowed it to search for security weaknesses.

According to Tenzai, the system was able to identify vulnerabilities while maintaining a false-positive rate of about 3.5%.

The company also said the latest run cost roughly 30% less per report than its previous run using US frontier AI models.

Tenzai's earlier tests showed that autonomous AI systems can identify complex vulnerabilities and combine multiple weaknesses into attack chains. The company has previously reported findings ranging from software vulnerabilities to remote-code-execution and database-access issues.

Open-weight models are becoming a cybersecurity issue

The result is significant because the models used by Tenzai are open-weight.

Unlike many commercial AI systems, open-weight models can be downloaded and run by developers and organisations without relying entirely on the model provider's online service.

This makes them easier to customise and deploy for different purposes.

It also means that the same technology can potentially be used by both defenders and attackers.

Tenzai CEO Pavel Gurvich has argued that open-weight models from China are already capable of performing sophisticated offensive cybersecurity tasks. The company said the models are not far behind leading US systems in cybersecurity-related capabilities.

The model is only part of the system

Tenzai said the HackerOne result does not necessarily mean that one AI model is simply better than another.

The company's system combines an AI model with an agentic security framework, which allows the AI to search for vulnerabilities, test potential weaknesses and produce reports.

Tenzai's CEO said the result demonstrated the importance of the system or "harness" surrounding the model, rather than just the underlying AI model itself.

This distinction is important because cybersecurity performance depends on more than a model's ability to understand code. The tools it can access, how it plans attacks, how it validates findings and how it interacts with target systems can all affect the final result.

Why open AI models matter to cybersecurity

The development creates a new challenge for security teams.

Powerful AI models that can be downloaded and operated outside a controlled commercial environment could allow organisations to build their own cybersecurity tools.

At the same time, the same capabilities could potentially be adapted for malicious purposes.

Recent research and industry testing have shown that increasingly capable AI agents can discover vulnerabilities, write code and automate parts of cyberattacks. Tenzai itself has reported that its AI hacker can continuously test applications and chain multiple vulnerabilities together.

This means defenders may need to consider AI not only as a security tool, but also as part of the changing threat landscape.

The race is moving beyond model development

The HackerOne results also show that the competition between AI systems is no longer limited to benchmarks that measure writing, reasoning or coding.

Cybersecurity is becoming another practical test of how well AI can operate in real environments.

For defenders, the development has two sides. AI can help security teams test more systems, identify vulnerabilities faster and reduce the cost of security testing.

But if similar tools become available to attackers, the speed at which vulnerabilities can be discovered and exploited could also increase.

As open-weight AI models become more capable and widely available, organisations may need to strengthen continuous vulnerability testing, access controls and monitoring to ensure that security weaknesses are discovered by defenders before attackers find them.
